notes: WHAT: A small standing man (about 30 cm tall) carved from pale gypsum alabaster, hands clasped at his chest, with huge staring eyes inlaid with shell and black limestone, a long beard once colored with bitumen, and a fringed skirt. Sumerian, Early Dynastic period, ca. 2900–2600 BCE, from southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq). The Met, 40.156. WHY IT MATTERS: Some of the oldest surviving statues of people were made not to be admired but to work. Sumerians placed figures like this in temples so that the statue could stand before the god and pray on the owner's behalf, day and night. Many were found buried together in temples such as the Square Temple at Tell Asmar (ancient Eshnunna). Art begins here as something useful and sacred, not as "decoration." HOW TO LOOK: (1) The eyes — enormous, wide open, never blinking: the figure must stay awake to keep praying. (2) The body is simplified into cones and cylinders; the sculptor cared about the idea "a person praying," not about real muscles. (3) The clasped hands — the whole pose is a gesture of devotion. ANECDOTE: The skirt is carved with a fringed hem, imitating the sheepskin or woolen garments Sumerians wore; even this tiny detail identified him as a worshiper. LINK: This is where our story starts — with a body that exists to pray, not to be beautiful.

illustrations.title: Standing male worshiper
illustrations.captionKo: 큰 눈으로 신을 바라보며 쉬지 않고 기도하는 작은 남자 조각상입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A small man with huge eyes, made to pray to the god day and night.

notes: WHAT: A marble female figure about 63 cm tall, standing with arms folded across her belly, head tilted back, nose the only facial feature carved, feet pointed downward. Early Cycladic II, ca. 2600–2400 BCE, from the Cycladic islands of the Aegean Sea (Greece). Attributed by scholars to an unknown carver called the "Bastis Master." The Met, 68.148. WHY IT MATTERS: This is one of the earliest nudes in our story. Cycladic figures are almost always female and naked, but they are not about seduction or real anatomy — the body is reduced to a few smooth, flat shapes. We still do not know exactly what they meant (goddess? ancestor? grave companion?). In the 20th century their pure, simple forms fascinated modern artists such as Brancusi and Modigliani. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The folded arms — the "canonical" Cycladic pose, right arm below left. (2) The pointed feet: she probably could not stand and was meant to lie down, perhaps in a grave. (3) Imagine her painted — scientists have found faint traces showing that eyes, hair and other details were once painted on the white marble. ANECDOTE: What looks to us like "minimalist modern art" is about 4,500 years old; the white blankness we admire is partly an accident of lost paint. LINK: Like the Sumerian worshiper, she is simplified into geometry — but here the subject is the naked female body, the beginning of our "nude" thread.

illustrations.title: Marble female figure
illustrations.captionKo: 팔짱을 낀 채 누워 있었을 것으로 보이는 아주 오래된 여인 조각입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A very old marble woman with folded arms, simple and smooth.

notes: WHAT: A small blue hippopotamus (20 cm long) made of faience — a glazed ceramic made from crushed quartz — painted with lotus flowers and river plants. Egypt, Middle Kingdom, Dynasty 12, ca. 1961–1878 BCE. Found in 1910 in a tomb at Meir in Middle Egypt (the tomb of a steward named Senbi). The Met, 17.9.1. WHY IT MATTERS: Egyptian art was made for eternity. Objects placed in tombs were meant to serve the dead in the afterlife. The hippo was both admired and feared: it lived in the Nile marshes and was one of the most dangerous animals in Egypt. Painting the marsh plants on its body turns the animal into a little world of the Nile. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The plants painted on its skin — the hippo carries its home on its back. (2) The intense blue-green, meant to suggest the river and new life. (3) The legs: three of the four are restored. Hippos like this were often deliberately broken, probably so they could not harm the dead person in the next world. ANECDOTE: The nickname "William" comes from a 1931 story in the British humor magazine Punch about a family who owned a picture of him. He is now the unofficial mascot of the Metropolitan Museum. LINK: From praying humans to a magical animal: in Egypt, too, art was made to do a job — here, to protect and accompany the dead.

illustrations.title: Hippopotamus ("William")
illustrations.captionKo: 연꽃 그림이 그려진 파란 하마, 메트로폴리탄 미술관의 마스코트 '윌리엄'입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A blue hippo painted with lotus flowers — the Met's mascot, "William."

notes: WHAT: A life-size seated statue (about 1.95 m) of Hatshepsut, who ruled Egypt as king ca. 1473–1458 BCE (New Kingdom, Dynasty 18). Indurated limestone with traces of paint. From her temple at Deir el-Bahri, western Thebes. The Met, 29.3.2. WHY IT MATTERS: Egyptian artists followed strict rules for the human figure for nearly 3,000 years: frontal, symmetrical, calm, built on a grid of fixed proportions. The goal was not a snapshot of a person but a permanent, perfect image that could last forever. Hatshepsut was a woman ruling as pharaoh, so her images normally show the male royal costume. This statue is unusual: she wears the king's striped nemes headcloth and kilt, yet her face and slender body are clearly feminine. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Perfect symmetry and stillness — hands flat on the knees, eyes forward: this is the "rule" of Egyptian art. (2) The mix of male regalia and a female body. (3) The block-like seat: the figure never quite escapes the stone. ANECDOTE: After her death, her successor Thutmose III had many of her statues smashed and thrown into a quarry near her temple. Excavators from The Met found most of this statue's pieces there in the 1920s (one fragment had been found by a German expedition in the 1840s) and fit them back together. LINK: The hippo served the dead; Hatshepsut's statue served power — and showed the Egyptian "canon" for the human body that the Greeks would later borrow and change.

illustrations.title: Seated Statue of Hatshepsut
illustrations.captionKo: 여성이면서 왕(파라오)이 된 하트셉수트의 좌상입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Hatshepsut, a woman who ruled Egypt as king, sits calm and still.

notes: WHAT: A colossal human-headed winged bull (lamassu), over 3 m tall and weighing about 7 tons, carved in gypsum alabaster. Neo-Assyrian, reign of Ashurnasirpal II, ca. 883–859 BCE. It guarded a doorway of his Northwest Palace at Nimrud (ancient Kalhu), in northern Iraq. The Met, 32.143.1. WHY IT MATTERS: Assyrian kings used art to show power. Protective spirits like this stood at palace gates to frighten enemies and evil forces. The lamassu combines the strength of a bull, the wings of an eagle and the intelligence of a man (with a horned crown showing divinity). HOW TO LOOK: (1) Count the legs — there are five. From the front it seems to stand firm; from the side it seems to stride forward. The sculptor designed it for two viewpoints. (2) The curls of the beard and the feathers — carved as neat, repeating patterns. (3) The cuneiform inscription carved between the legs, which praises the king. ANECDOTE: Hauling these giants from Nimrud was a huge 19th‑century undertaking. The Met's pair came as a gift of John D. Rockefeller Jr. in 1932. LINK: Like Hatshepsut's statue, it shows royal power — but here art is a monster-guardian, built to impress anyone walking through the door.

illustrations.title: Human-headed winged bull (lamassu)
illustrations.captionKo: 사람 얼굴과 날개를 가진 거대한 황소가 궁전 문을 지키고 있습니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A giant winged bull with a man's face guards a palace door.

notes: WHAT: A life-size marble statue (about 1.95 m) of a kouros — a naked young man — standing with left foot forward, arms at his sides, fists clenched. Greek, Attic, ca. 590–580 BCE, carved from Naxian marble. One of the earliest marble statues of a human figure made in Attica (the region of Athens). The Met, 32.11.1. WHY IT MATTERS: The Greeks learned monumental stone sculpture partly from Egypt — the pose and even the proportions follow the Egyptian grid. But one thing is completely new: he is naked. For the Greeks, the nude male body expressed excellence, youth and the ideal citizen-athlete. This is where the Western idea of the ideal nude begins. Such statues often stood over graves or were offered to gods. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Compare with Hatshepsut: same frontal stance and forward foot, but now the stone is cut away between the arms and body and between the legs — he is freed from the block. (2) The knees, ribs and stomach are drawn as patterns rather than real anatomy. (3) The beaded hair and the faint "archaic" stillness of the face. ANECDOTE: Over the next 100 years, Greek sculptors changed these stiff youths step by step into relaxed, natural bodies — one of the fastest revolutions in art history. LINK: Egypt gave the pose; Greece added the naked body as an ideal — the true start of our nude thread.

illustrations.title: Marble statue of a kouros (youth)
illustrations.captionKo: 왼발을 앞으로 내민 벌거벗은 그리스 청년상, '쿠로스'입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A naked Greek youth, a "kouros," steps forward with his left foot.

notes: WHAT: A marble grave marker (stele), about 80 cm tall, showing a little girl holding two doves; she lifts one close to her face as if to kiss it. Greek, Classical period, ca. 450–440 BCE, carved in marble from the island of Paros. The Met, 27.45. WHY IT MATTERS: In the 5th century BCE, Greek artists learned to show not only perfect bodies but also feeling — quietly. This relief marked a child's grave. There is no dramatic weeping; instead, a tender everyday moment speaks of love and loss. The figure is shown in natural profile, her dress falling in soft, believable folds — something the stiff kouros could not do. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The drapery: thin cloth that reveals the shape of the body underneath. (2) The gesture of the hands and the dove near her lips — intimate and calm. (3) Her profile — head slightly bent, a classic Greek expression of gentle sadness. ANECDOTE: Grave reliefs like this lined the roads outside Greek cities, so passers-by would "meet" the dead. This one was likely painted, and the doves may have been her pets. LINK: In about 130 years, Greek art moved from the frozen kouros to this soft, living gesture.

illustrations.title: Marble grave stele of a little girl
illustrations.captionKo: 비둘기 두 마리를 안은 어린 소녀를 새긴 그리스의 무덤 비석입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A Greek grave marker: a little girl gently holds two doves.

notes: WHAT: A marble statue of the Diadoumenos — a victorious young athlete tying a ribbon (fillet) around his head. This is a Roman copy (Flavian period, ca. 69–96 CE) of a famous lost bronze made around 430 BCE by the Greek sculptor Polykleitos of Argos. The Met, 25.78.56 (restored from fragments). WHY IT MATTERS: Polykleitos wrote a treatise called the Canon, explaining how to build a perfect body from mathematical proportions between its parts. His statues show contrapposto: weight on one leg, the other relaxed, so hips and shoulders tilt in opposite directions. This balanced, living pose became the model of "classical beauty" for the next 2,500 years — from Michelangelo to modern fashion photos. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Weight on the right leg; left leg bent and resting — notice the tilted hips. (2) The calm, almost expressionless face: the beauty is in the body's harmony, not emotion. (3) The raised arms framing the head — he is tying the victor's ribbon. ANECDOTE: Almost all great Greek bronzes were melted down long ago. We know them mainly through Roman marble copies like this one; the tree-trunk support was added because marble cannot stand on thin legs the way bronze can. LINK: The kouros stood stiff; the Diadoumenos stands relaxed — the classical ideal of the male nude is now complete.

illustrations.title: Fragments of a marble statue of the Diadoumenos (youth tying a fillet around his head)
illustrations.captionKo: 승리의 리본을 머리에 묶는 젊은 운동선수, 고전적인 '이상적 몸'의 본보기입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A young athlete ties a victory ribbon — a model of the ideal classical body.

notes: WHAT: A marble statue of Aphrodite, goddess of love, standing naked, with a dolphin beside her leg (a sign of her birth from the sea). Roman, 1st or 2nd century CE, copying a Greek statue type. The Met, 52.11.5. WHY IT MATTERS: For centuries Greek sculptors showed men naked but women clothed. Around 350 BCE the Athenian sculptor Praxiteles made the Aphrodite of Knidos — the first famous life-size fully nude female statue. Statues like this Roman one belong to the tradition it started. Here the female nude becomes a subject of beauty and admiration — and the long story of "Venus" begins. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The gentle S-curve of the body and the weight on one leg (contrapposto, now softened). (2) The dolphin support: a practical brace for the marble, but also a clue to her identity. (3) Compare with the Cycladic figure: real flesh, soft transitions, a body meant to be looked at. ANECDOTE: According to the Roman writer Pliny, Praxiteles offered two versions of Aphrodite; the people of Kos chose the modest, clothed one, while the city of Knidos took the nude — and it became so famous that travelers sailed there just to see it. LINK: The Diadoumenos gave the ideal male nude; Aphrodite opens the long tradition of the ideal female nude that will lead to Botticelli, Titian and beyond.

illustrations.title: Marble statue of Aphrodite
illustrations.artist: Unknown Roman sculptor, after a Greek original
illustrations.captionKo: 바다에서 태어난 사랑의 여신 아프로디테, 옆에 돌고래가 있습니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Aphrodite, goddess of love, stands with a dolphin from the sea.

notes: WHAT: A complete Roman bedroom (cubiculum) with its original wall paintings, from the Villa of Publius Fannius Synistor at Boscoreale, near Pompeii. Fresco, painted ca. 50–40 BCE. Installed as a room you can walk into at The Met, 03.14.13a–g. WHY IT MATTERS: Romans decorated their homes with painted "windows" onto imaginary worlds. In this so-called Second Style, painters used light, shadow and overlapping forms to make flat walls look as if they opened onto city views, columned buildings, gardens and a rocky grotto with a fountain. It shows that ancient painters already understood illusion and depth — knowledge largely lost in the Middle Ages and rediscovered in the Renaissance. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Stand in the center: the painted buildings seem to go back into space. (2) Look for still-life details — a glass bowl of fruit, birds, a fountain. (3) Notice the real window at the end of the room, set among the painted "windows." ANECDOTE: The villa was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, which preserved the paintings under ash. It was excavated around 1900. LINK: From marble bodies to painted space: the Romans pushed illusion — making a wall into a view.

illustrations.title: Cubiculum (bedroom) from the Villa of P. Fannius Synistor at Boscoreale
illustrations.captionKo: 폼페이 근처 별장의 침실 벽에 그려진, 깊이감 있는 로마 벽화입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A Roman bedroom near Pompeii, its walls painted with deep, open views.

notes: WHAT: A portrait of a young woman in a red tunic with a gold leaf wreath in her dark hair, painted on a thin limewood panel. Encaustic (pigment mixed with hot wax) with gold leaf. Roman Egypt, 90–120 CE. The Met, 09.181.6. WHY IT MATTERS: In Roman-period Egypt, wealthy people combined Egyptian mummification with Roman realistic portraiture. A painted portrait was wrapped into the mummy bandages over the face. These "Fayum portraits" (named after the region where many were found) are among the most lifelike faces surviving from the ancient world — individual, alert and strikingly modern. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The eyes: large, dark, and directly meeting ours. (2) Highlights on the nose and lips — the painter modeled the face with light and shadow. (3) The real gold leaf in the wreath and jewelry, which catches light. ANECDOTE: Encaustic painting uses melted beeswax, which is why the colors still look fresh after nearly 2,000 years. LINK: The Boscoreale walls showed space; this panel shows a real person's face — the last flowering of ancient realism before medieval art turned toward symbols.

illustrations.title: Portrait of a young woman in red
illustrations.captionKo: 미라 얼굴 위에 놓였던, 빨간 옷을 입은 젊은 여인의 초상입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A young woman in red, painted to cover her face on her mummy.

notes: WHAT: The Chi-Rho page (folio 34r) of the Book of Kells, an illuminated manuscript of the four Gospels in Latin, made around 800 CE by monks, probably at Iona (Scotland) and/or Kells (Ireland). Ink and pigments on vellum (calfskin). Trinity College Library, Dublin. WHY IT MATTERS: After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, monasteries kept learning alive by copying books by hand. Insular (Irish and British) artists combined Celtic spirals and knots with Christian text. This page opens Matthew's account of Christ's birth with the Greek letters Chi (X) and Rho (P), the first letters of "Christ," turned into a dazzling field of pattern. The goal is not realism but glory — the word itself becomes holy art. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Find the giant X shape and the P below it. (2) Lean in: the spirals and knots are tiny and never repeat exactly. (3) Hidden animals — near the bottom, cats watch mice nibbling a round wafer; elsewhere there are moths and an otter holding a fish. ANECDOTE: The book has been at Trinity College Dublin since the 17th century; today it is displayed with pages turned regularly, and it draws huge crowds every year. LINK: The lifelike Fayum face gives way to a page of pure pattern — medieval art cares more about meaning than about copying the visible world.

illustrations.title: Chi-Rho page, Book of Kells (folio 34r)
illustrations.credit: Trinity College Library, Dublin, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 그리스도의 이름 첫 글자를 화려한 무늬로 채운 『켈스의 서』의 한 페이지입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A page of the Book of Kells, where the first letters of "Christ" become rich patterns.

notes: WHAT: A small painting of the Virgin Mary holding the Christ Child, who reaches up to pull at her veil. Tempera and gold on wood, ca. 1290–1300, by Duccio di Buoninsegna of Siena. Only about 28 × 21 cm including its original frame. The Met, 2004.442. WHY IT MATTERS: Duccio worked within the Byzantine tradition — gold background, flat holy figures — but he added human tenderness: the baby plays with his mother's veil, and Mary looks sad, as if she already knows his fate. At the bottom is a painted parapet (a low ledge), a step toward placing figures in real space, in front of the viewer. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The child's hand tugging the veil — a tiny, human gesture. (2) The parapet at the bottom: where our world meets theirs. (3) The original frame: look for small burn marks, likely from candles lit during private prayer. ANECDOTE: When The Met bought it in 2004, it was reported to cost about $45 million, the most the museum had ever paid for a painting — for a work smaller than a sheet of paper. LINK: From the abstract glory of the Book of Kells to a mother and child who feel like real people — the first sign of a new age.

illustrations.title: Madonna and Child
illustrations.captionKo: 아기 예수가 엄마의 베일을 잡아당기는, 금빛 배경의 작은 성모자상입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A tiny gold painting: baby Jesus tugs at his mother's veil.

notes: WHAT: The Hours of Jeanne d'Evreux, a tiny prayer book (each page about 9 × 6 cm) painted by Jean Pucelle in Paris around 1324–28 for Jeanne d'Evreux, queen of France (wife of King Charles IV). Grisaille (painting in shades of gray), tempera and ink on vellum. The Met Cloisters, 54.1.2. WHY IT MATTERS: A "book of hours" contained prayers for different times of the day, used by wealthy lay people. Pucelle painted mostly in soft grays, which makes the figures look like little sculptures, with touches of color. He also borrowed ideas of space from Italian painters such as Duccio — rooms and buildings that people can stand inside. The margins are full of drolleries: playful figures, animals and jokes, mixing the sacred and the silly. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The gray "sculptural" figures. (2) The little architectural boxes that create space. (3) The margins — musicians, animals, games, small surprises. ANECDOTE: The queen valued the book so much that she left it in her will to King Charles V. It survived the centuries and was acquired by The Met Cloisters in 1954. LINK: Duccio's new space travels north: a French artist shrinks it into a book that fits in your palm.

illustrations.title: The Hours of Jeanne d'Evreux, Queen of France
illustrations.captionKo: 손바닥만 한 왕비의 기도서, 회색 톤으로 섬세하게 그렸습니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A queen's palm-sized prayer book, painted in soft shades of gray.

notes: WHAT: The January page from the Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry, a book of hours painted around 1412–16 by the Limbourg brothers (Paul, Herman and Jean) for Jean, Duke of Berry, a brother of the French king. Pigments and gold on vellum. Musée Condé, Chantilly (France). WHY IT MATTERS: This is the high point of "International Gothic" — elegant, colorful, full of luxury. The calendar pages show the months through scenes of court life and peasant work, in rich detail. January shows a New Year's feast: the duke, in blue, sits at the table, while servants bring food and guests crowd in to exchange gifts. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The duke, with a round fire screen behind his head like a halo. (2) The tapestry on the wall showing knights in battle. (3) The little dogs on the table and the zodiac signs in the half-circle above. ANECDOTE: Above the duke, a courtier's words "Approche, approche" ("come closer, come closer") are written — inviting guests (and us) into the feast. The brothers died in 1416, probably of plague, and the book was finished by other artists decades later. LINK: Pucelle's queenly prayer book grows into the most famous illuminated manuscript in Europe — a mirror of courtly splendor.

illustrations.title: January, from Les Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry
illustrations.credit: Musée Condé, Chantilly, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 1월 새해 잔치를 즐기는 베리 공작과 손님들의 화려한 모습입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: The Duke of Berry enjoys a rich New Year's feast in January.

notes: WHAT: "The Unicorn Rests in a Garden," the last and most famous of the seven Unicorn Tapestries. Wool warp with wool, silk, silver and gilt wefts. Designed in France and woven in the Southern Netherlands, 1495–1505. The Met Cloisters, 37.80.6. WHY IT MATTERS: Tapestries were among the most expensive art forms of the late Middle Ages — warm, portable and luxurious. In this scene the unicorn, a legendary animal that only a pure maiden could tame, sits chained to a pomegranate tree inside a small round fence. It can be read as Christ resurrected, or as a symbol of a faithful lover or marriage — likely both meanings were intended. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The red drops on the unicorn's white coat — juice from the bursting pomegranates above, a symbol of fertility, not blood. (2) The "millefleurs" (thousand flowers) background: scholars have identified dozens of real plant species. (3) The loose chain and low fence — he could leave, but chooses to stay. ANECDOTE: According to tradition, during the French Revolution the tapestries were taken from a château and used to cover potatoes. John D. Rockefeller Jr. bought them and gave them to The Met in 1937. LINK: The end of the Middle Ages — still full of symbols, but every flower now looks observed from nature. The Renaissance is near.

illustrations.title: The Unicorn Rests in a Garden (from the Unicorn Tapestries)
illustrations.captionKo: 수천 송이 꽃밭 한가운데 울타리 안에서 쉬고 있는 유니콘입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A unicorn rests inside a small fence in a field of a thousand flowers.

notes: WHAT: "The Lamentation (The Mourning of Christ)," a fresco painted around 1305 by Giotto di Bondone in the Arena (Scrovegni) Chapel in Padua, Italy. The chapel was commissioned by the banker Enrico Scrovegni and is covered with Giotto's scenes of the lives of Mary and Christ. WHY IT MATTERS: Giotto is often called the father of Western painting. He gave figures real weight and volume — they sit on the ground, turn their backs, and express grief with their whole bodies. Instead of gold backgrounds, he painted a simple blue sky and a rocky landscape. People feel like actors on a stage, and we feel like witnesses. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The two figures seated with their backs to us — we cannot see their faces, yet we feel their sorrow, and they pull us into the circle. (2) The diagonal rock edge that leads our eye down to the faces of Mary and Christ. (3) The angels in the sky, each twisting in a different pose of despair. ANECDOTE: The 16th‑century writer Giorgio Vasari tells a legend that when the pope asked for a sample of Giotto's skill, Giotto drew a perfect circle freehand. LINK: From the flat elegance of Gothic manuscripts to solid human bodies and real emotion — the Renaissance begins in Italy.

illustrations.title: Lamentation (The Mourning of Christ)
illustrations.credit: Scrovegni (Arena) Chapel, Padua, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 예수의 죽음을 슬퍼하는 사람들을 무게감 있게 그린 조토의 벽화입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Giotto's fresco: people mourn the dead Christ with real, heavy bodies.

notes: WHAT: "The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden," a fresco by Masaccio painted around 1424–27 in the Brancacci Chapel, Santa Maria del Carmine, Florence. Adam and Eve, naked, walk out of Paradise under a sword-bearing angel. WHY IT MATTERS: Masaccio, who died at about 26, painted the most emotional nudes since antiquity. These are not ideal statues but real people in despair: Adam covers his face; Eve screams with an open mouth. Light falls from one direction and casts shadows, giving the bodies weight. Masaccio was also a pioneer of linear perspective, the new mathematics of space developed in Florence. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Eve's pose: her arms cover breasts and lap — borrowed from the ancient "modest Venus" (Venus Pudica) statue type, but turned into shame and grief. (2) Adam's hidden face — sorrow too great to show. (3) The shadows cast on the ground. ANECDOTE: In the 17th century, fig leaves were painted over their bodies. A restoration completed around 1990 removed them, revealing the nudity Masaccio intended. LINK: Giotto gave bodies weight; Masaccio gives the naked body tragic feeling — the nude returns to Western art.

illustrations.title: The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden
illustrations.credit: Brancacci Chapel, Santa Maria del Carmine, Florence, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 낙원에서 쫓겨나며 울부짖는 아담과 이브의 모습입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Adam and Eve cry out in grief as they leave Paradise.

notes: WHAT: "The Birth of Venus," tempera on canvas, painted by Sandro Botticelli around 1484–86 in Florence, probably for a member of the Medici family circle. Uffizi Gallery, Florence. Venus, goddess of love, arrives on a scallop shell, blown to shore by the wind god Zephyr (with a female companion), while a nymph of spring rushes to cover her with a flowered cloak. WHY IT MATTERS: This is one of the first large paintings since antiquity to show a naked goddess from classical myth as its main subject. Florentine scholars of the time believed ancient beauty could lead the soul toward the divine, so a pagan Venus could also stand for spiritual, ideal love. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Her pose copies the ancient "modest Venus" (compare Eve in the last chapter), but here it is calm and dreamy. (2) The impossible anatomy — a very long neck, sloping shoulders, weight on one leg that couldn't really hold her: Botticelli chose graceful line over correct anatomy. (3) The roses floating in the air and the gold highlights. ANECDOTE: Vasari reports that later in life Botticelli fell under the influence of the fiery preacher Savonarola, who condemned worldly and pagan art in Florence. LINK: Masaccio's Eve was naked in shame; Botticelli's Venus is naked in beauty — the classical goddess is reborn.

illustrations.captionKo: 조개껍데기를 타고 바다에서 태어나 육지에 도착하는 비너스입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Venus is born from the sea and arrives on a shell.

notes: WHAT: The "Mona Lisa," oil on poplar panel, by Leonardo da Vinci, begun around 1503 and worked on for many years (until about 1519). The sitter is generally identified as Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo (hence "La Gioconda"). Musée du Louvre, Paris. WHY IT MATTERS: Leonardo invented a new way of making a face feel alive. He used sfumato ("smoky") — soft, gradual shading without hard outlines, especially at the corners of the mouth and eyes. Because those edges are blurred, her expression seems to change as we look. The three-quarter pose with folded hands became a model for portraits for centuries. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The corners of the mouth and eyes — no lines, only shadows. (2) The landscape: the horizon on the left looks lower than on the right, which adds to the strange, shifting effect. (3) Her hands, relaxed and beautifully modeled. ANECDOTE: In 1911 an Italian handyman, Vincenzo Peruggia, stole it from the Louvre; it was recovered in Florence in 1913. The theft made it the most famous painting in the world. LINK: Botticelli drew elegant lines; Leonardo dissolved the lines into soft light and shadow — the High Renaissance begins.

illustrations.title: Mona Lisa
illustrations.credit: Musée du Louvre, Paris, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 부드러운 그림자로 신비로운 미소를 만든 레오나르도의 '모나리자'입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Leonardo's Mona Lisa, with a mysterious smile made of soft shadows.

notes: WHAT: "The Creation of Adam," one of the central scenes on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican, painted in fresco by Michelangelo Buonarroti between 1508 and 1512 for Pope Julius II. God, carried by angels in a billowing cloak, reaches toward the reclining Adam, whose finger is about to receive the spark of life. WHY IT MATTERS: Michelangelo considered himself a sculptor first, and he paints bodies as if they were carved. Adam is the ideal male nude of the Renaissance — a revival of the Greek ideal (think of the Diadoumenos) charged with new power and emotion. Michelangelo believed the beautiful human body was the clearest reflection of God's creation. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The gap between the two fingers — the most famous empty space in art. (2) Adam's limp, waiting body vs. God's energetic rush. (3) The young figure under God's arm, whom some scholars identify as Eve, not yet created, looking at Adam. ANECDOTE: Contrary to popular belief, Michelangelo did not paint lying on his back; he stood on a scaffold and bent backward. He wrote a comic poem complaining about the pain in his neck and back. LINK: Leonardo explored softness and mystery; Michelangelo returns to the heroic nude body — the Greek ideal reborn on a giant scale.

illustrations.title: The Creation of Adam (Sistine Chapel ceiling)
illustrations.credit: Sistine Chapel, Vatican City, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 하나님이 아담에게 생명을 주려고 손가락을 뻗는 장면입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: God reaches out his finger to give life to Adam.

notes: WHAT: "The School of Athens," a fresco by Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio) painted 1509–1511 in the Stanza della Segnatura, a room in the papal apartments of the Vatican, for Pope Julius II. Ancient Greek philosophers gather in a grand vaulted hall. WHY IT MATTERS: Raphael brings together everything the Renaissance had learned — perspective, balanced composition, natural poses and calm dignity. At the center walk Plato, pointing up to the world of ideas, and Aristotle, holding his hand flat toward the real world. Around them, dozens of thinkers form harmonious groups. It is a picture of the Renaissance belief that ancient wisdom and Christian culture could live together. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Follow the floor and ceiling lines: they meet at a vanishing point between Plato and Aristotle. (2) Plato's face is traditionally said to be modeled on Leonardo da Vinci. (3) Near the bottom, a brooding figure leaning on a block (Heraclitus) is often identified as a portrait of Michelangelo, added after Raphael saw the Sistine ceiling. ANECDOTE: Raphael included himself at the far right edge, looking out at us — a young artist signing his place among the great minds. LINK: Michelangelo's power and Leonardo's grace meet in Raphael's perfect harmony.

illustrations.title: The School of Athens
illustrations.credit: Vatican Museums (Stanza della Segnatura), Vatican City, via Wikimedia Commons

illustrations.captionEn: Ancient thinkers, led by Plato and Aristotle, gather in a grand hall.

notes: WHAT: The "Venus of Urbino," oil on canvas, painted by Titian (Tiziano Vecellio) in Venice in 1538, bought by Guidobaldo della Rovere, who became Duke of Urbino. Uffizi Gallery, Florence. A naked woman reclines on a white sheet in a rich palace bedroom, holding roses, a small dog asleep at her feet; in the background two maids search a chest. WHY IT MATTERS: Venetian painters built pictures with color and glowing oil glazes rather than line. Titian took the reclining nude from his teacher-colleague Giorgione's "Sleeping Venus" (shown as a second image here, ca. 1510), but moved her indoors and — crucially — opened her eyes. She looks straight at the viewer. Is she a goddess or a real woman in a real room? This ambiguity created the template for the reclining nude for 300 years — the direct ancestor of Manet's Olympia. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Her direct gaze. (2) The dog, often read as a symbol of fidelity, and the chest (cassone), linked to marriage. (3) The warm skin against the cool white sheets and dark background. ANECDOTE: Mark Twain, visiting the Uffizi, called it "the foulest, the vilest, the obscenest picture the world possesses" in A Tramp Abroad (1880). LINK: Botticelli's Venus stood on the sea; Titian's lies on a bed and looks back at us.

illustrations.title: Venus of Urbino
illustrations.credit: Uffizi Gallery, Florence, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 침대에 누워 우리를 바라보는 티치아노의 비너스입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Titian's Venus lies on a bed and looks right at us.
