illustrations.captionEn: Compare Giorgione's Venus, asleep with her eyes closed outdoors.

notes: WHAT: "The Arnolfini Portrait," oil on oak panel, painted by Jan van Eyck in Bruges (Flanders) in 1434. National Gallery, London. A richly dressed merchant, usually identified as Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini of Lucca, and a woman stand hand in hand in a bedroom, a small dog at their feet. WHY IT MATTERS: Van Eyck perfected oil painting: thin transparent layers (glazes) that let him render every material — fur, brass, glass, wood, wool — with amazing truth. While Italians studied ideal forms and perspective, Northern painters observed every detail of the visible world. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The convex mirror on the back wall: it reflects the couple from behind and two more figures in the doorway — maybe the painter himself. Around its frame are ten tiny scenes of Christ's Passion. (2) The signature above the mirror: "Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434" ("Jan van Eyck was here 1434"). (3) A single candle burning in the chandelier in daylight, and the shoes left on the floor. ANECDOTE: Scholars still debate what the painting records — a marriage, a betrothal, or a memorial — showing how many meanings can hide in everyday objects. LINK: Italy reinvented the body; the North reinvented the eye — painting the world in microscopic detail.

illustrations.title: The Arnolfini Portrait
illustrations.credit: National Gallery, London, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 손을 맞잡은 부부와 뒤쪽 볼록 거울이 유명한 얀 반 에이크의 그림입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A couple holds hands; look for the famous round mirror behind them.

notes: WHAT: "The Garden of Earthly Delights," a triptych (three-panel altarpiece-like painting) in oil on oak by Hieronymus Bosch, painted around 1490–1510 in 's-Hertogenbosch (the Netherlands). Museo del Prado, Madrid. WHY IT MATTERS: Bosch created one of the strangest and most imaginative works in Western art. Left panel: God presents Eve to Adam in Paradise. Center: a vast garden full of naked men and women playing with giant fruits, birds and strange structures — pleasure without shame, or sin? Right panel: a dark, burning Hell with musical instruments used as torture devices. The bodies here are not ideal nudes; they are small, pale and countless — humanity itself. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Read left to right: Paradise → earthly pleasure → Hell. (2) The giant strawberries and fruits, symbols of short-lived pleasure. (3) In Hell, find the "tree-man," whose hollow body holds a tavern — perhaps a self-portrait. ANECDOTE: When closed, the outer wings show the world in gray tones as a transparent globe on the third day of creation. The painting was later owned by King Philip II of Spain. LINK: Van Eyck painted the real world; Bosch used the same skill to paint dreams and nightmares.

illustrations.title: The Garden of Earthly Delights
illustrations.credit: Museo del Prado, Madrid, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 낙원, 쾌락의 정원, 지옥을 세 폭에 그린 보스의 신비한 그림입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Bosch's three panels: Paradise, a garden of pleasure, and Hell.

notes: WHAT: "Adam and Eve," an engraving by Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg, 1504. The Met, 19.73.1. Adam and Eve stand naked in a dark forest; Eve takes the forbidden fruit from the serpent while animals surround them. WHY IT MATTERS: Dürer traveled to Italy and became obsessed with the Italian and ancient secret of ideal proportions. This print is his demonstration of the perfect male and female body, built from measured proportions; Adam's pose recalls the famous ancient Apollo Belvedere. Because prints could be made in many copies, Dürer spread the Renaissance ideal nude across Northern Europe. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Both figures stand in contrapposto, like Greek statues (compare the Diadoumenos). (2) The animals: an elk, ox, rabbit and cat were understood to stand for the four "temperaments" (moods) that, according to medieval thinking, fell out of balance after the Fall. (3) The cat about to pounce on the mouse at Adam's feet — the moment before sin. ANECDOTE: Dürer proudly signed it on a little tablet hanging from a branch: "ALBERT DURER NORICUS FACIEBAT 1504" ("Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg made this, 1504"). He also famously painted himself in a Christ-like frontal pose (1500) — an artist who knew his own worth. LINK: Bosch's naked crowds were sinners; Dürer's Adam and Eve are perfect bodies — the Italian ideal moves north.

illustrations.title: Adam and Eve
illustrations.captionKo: 뒤러가 '완벽한 비율'로 새긴 아담과 이브의 판화입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Dürer's print of Adam and Eve, made with "perfect" proportions.

notes: WHAT: "The Harvesters," oil on wood, by Pieter Bruegel the Elder, 1565. The Met, 19.164. Peasants cut and bundle golden wheat; others rest under a pear tree, eating bread, cheese and porridge, while one man sleeps sprawled on the ground. The landscape opens out to a distant bay. WHY IT MATTERS: It is one of a series of six paintings of the times of the year that Bruegel made for the Antwerp merchant Niclaes Jongelinck (five survive). Bruegel made ordinary farm workers and the landscape itself the subject of a major painting — no saints, no gods. It is one of the founding works of Western landscape painting. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Follow the path cut through the wheat into the distance. (2) The lunch group: each person is doing something different — eating, drinking, slicing bread. (3) Tiny distant details: a church, a ship on the water, people playing a game. ANECDOTE: The Met bought the painting in 1919. It is the only one of the surviving five in the series that is not in Europe. LINK: Dürer studied the ideal body; Bruegel looked at real, tired, hungry bodies in a real landscape.

illustrations.title: The Harvesters
illustrations.captionKo: 황금빛 밀밭에서 일하고 쉬는 농부들의 여름 오후입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Farmers work and rest in a golden wheat field on a summer day.

notes: WHAT: "The Calling of Saint Matthew," oil on canvas, by Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio, 1599–1600, painted for the Contarelli Chapel in the church of San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome, where it still hangs. Christ enters a dim room where the tax collector Matthew sits counting money with companions, and points to him: "Follow me." WHY IT MATTERS: Caravaggio shocked Rome by painting holy stories with ordinary people in contemporary clothes, in dark rooms cut by dramatic light. This strong contrast of light and dark (chiaroscuro, pushed to "tenebrism") became the signature of Baroque painting across Europe. Religion is no longer distant and golden; it happens in a tavern-like room, right now. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The beam of light from the upper right, running parallel to Christ's pointing arm — light itself is the calling. (2) Christ's hand: it echoes Adam's hand in Michelangelo's Creation of Adam (Chapter 21). (3) Who is Matthew? Most see the bearded man pointing to himself ("Me?"); some argue it is the young man bent over the coins. ANECDOTE: Caravaggio's life was as dramatic as his painting: in 1606 he killed a man in a brawl and fled Rome, spending his last years on the run. He died in 1610, about 38 years old. LINK: From Bruegel's daylight fields to Caravaggio's spotlight — the Baroque age of drama begins.

illustrations.title: The Calling of Saint Matthew
illustrations.credit: Contarelli Chapel, San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 어두운 방에 빛이 들어오며 예수가 마태오를 부르는 순간입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Light enters a dark room as Jesus calls Matthew.

notes: WHAT: "Judith Slaying Holofernes," oil on canvas, by Artemisia Gentileschi, painted around 1620 in Florence. Uffizi Gallery, Florence. The biblical heroine Judith, helped by her maid Abra, beheads the enemy general Holofernes to save her people. WHY IT MATTERS: Artemisia was one of the first women to build a successful career as a painter in Europe and, in 1616, the first woman admitted to Florence's Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. She learned Caravaggio's dramatic light from her father, Orazio, a follower of Caravaggio. Her version of this popular subject is unusually physical: the women are strong, determined and fully in action — not delicate or hesitant. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The triangle of arms at the center, all pushing toward Holofernes's head. (2) The maid actively holding him down — in many other versions she only waits with a bag. (3) The arcs of blood and the crisp light on the white sheets. ANECDOTE: In 1612 Artemisia's father took the painter Agostino Tassi to court for raping her; during the trial she was tortured with thumbscrews to "test" her testimony. Many viewers see her powerful Judiths in the light of this story, though she painted many other subjects too. LINK: Caravaggio's dramatic light, seen through the eyes of a woman artist — the body becomes a site of action and force.

illustrations.title: Judith Slaying Holofernes
illustrations.credit: Uffizi Gallery, Florence, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 유디트와 하녀가 힘을 합쳐 적장을 물리치는 극적인 장면입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Judith and her maid bravely overpower the enemy general.

notes: WHAT: "Venus and Adonis," oil on canvas, by Peter Paul Rubens, probably mid-1630s. The Met, 37.162. Venus, goddess of love, clings to the young hunter Adonis, begging him not to go hunting; little Cupid grabs his leg. Adonis, with his dogs, is about to leave — and, as Ovid's Metamorphoses tells, he will be killed by a wild boar. WHY IT MATTERS: Rubens, from Antwerp, was the great painter of Baroque energy: swirling movement, rich color and warm, full-bodied flesh. His Venus is soft, rounded and glowing — so typical that "Rubenesque" became a word for a full female figure. Rubens had studied Titian in Italy and Spain, and this composition is based on Titian's own "Venus and Adonis." HOW TO LOOK: (1) The diagonal pull between the two bodies — love holding back, duty pulling away. (2) The skin: Rubens layered pinks, creams and even blues to make flesh look alive. (3) Cupid's desperate grip on Adonis's leg. ANECDOTE: Rubens was also a diplomat who negotiated peace between Spain and England; he was knighted by both King Philip IV of Spain and King Charles I of England. LINK: Artemisia showed bodies in violent action; Rubens shows the nude full of warmth, color and movement — the Baroque Venus.

illustrations.title: Venus and Adonis
illustrations.captionKo: 사냥을 떠나려는 아도니스를 붙잡는 비너스와 큐피드입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Venus and little Cupid try to stop Adonis from going hunting.

notes: WHAT: "The Toilet of Venus," known as the "Rokeby Venus," oil on canvas, by Diego Velázquez, painted around 1647–51. National Gallery, London. Venus lies on a dark sheet with her back to us, while Cupid holds a mirror in which we see her face. WHY IT MATTERS: In Catholic Spain, the Inquisition strongly discouraged nude paintings, which makes this the only surviving female nude by Velázquez. Instead of a frontal goddess, he paints a real-looking woman from behind, with fluid, loose brushwork. The mirror makes the picture about looking: she seems to watch us watching her. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The long curve of her back and hip against the gray-white and dark sheets. (2) The mirror: her face is blurred, and — if you think about the angle — she would actually be seeing us, not herself. (3) The pink ribbons of Cupid, almost a single flick of the brush. ANECDOTE: In 1914 the suffragette Mary Richardson attacked the painting with a meat cleaver, slashing it several times, to protest the arrest of suffrage leader Emmeline Pankhurst. She later said she disliked the way men gaped at it. It was restored. Its nickname comes from Rokeby Park in northern England, where it hung in the 19th century. LINK: Rubens's Venus moves toward us; Velázquez's turns away — and the question "who is looking?" enters the nude thread.

illustrations.title: The Toilet of Venus (The Rokeby Venus)
illustrations.credit: National Gallery, London, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 등을 돌린 비너스가 큐피드가 든 거울 속에서 우리를 바라봅니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Venus turns her back, and her face looks at us from a mirror.

notes: WHAT: "Bathsheba at Her Bath," oil on canvas, by Rembrandt van Rijn, 1654. Musée du Louvre, Paris. In the Bible, King David sees Bathsheba bathing and sends a letter summoning her, though she is married. Rembrandt shows her seated, naked, holding the letter, while an old maid dries her feet. WHY IT MATTERS: Instead of an ideal goddess, Rembrandt paints a real woman's body — soft belly, ordinary proportions — and, above all, her thoughts. She is not posing for us; she is thinking about a terrible choice. The nude becomes psychological. The model is generally thought to have been Hendrickje Stoffels, Rembrandt's companion. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Her lowered eyes and quiet, sad face. (2) The letter in her hand — the whole story in one small piece of paper. (3) The warm golden light on her skin against the dark background. Compare with the second image, Rembrandt's own Self-Portrait of 1660 (The Met): the same honesty applied to his aging face. ANECDOTE: In 1654, the same year, Hendrickje, pregnant and unmarried to Rembrandt, was summoned before the church council of the Reformed Church in Amsterdam and reprimanded for living with him. LINK: Velázquez turned the nude into a game of mirrors; Rembrandt turns it inward, toward a human mind.

illustrations.title: Bathsheba at Her Bath
illustrations.credit: Musée du Louvre, Paris, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 다윗 왕의 편지를 들고 깊은 생각에 잠긴 밧세바입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Bathsheba holds King David's letter, lost in thought.

illustrations.title: Self-Portrait
illustrations.captionKo: 같은 정직함으로 그린 렘브란트의 노년 자화상입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Rembrandt painted his own aging face with the same honesty.

notes: WHAT: "Las Meninas" ("The Ladies-in-Waiting"), oil on canvas, by Diego Velázquez, 1656. Museo del Prado, Madrid. The little Infanta (princess) Margarita Teresa stands in a large room of the royal palace, surrounded by her maids of honor (meninas), a dwarf, a dog and others. On the left, Velázquez himself stands with brush and palette before a huge canvas. WHY IT MATTERS: It is one of the most discussed paintings ever made, because it is a painting about seeing. In the mirror at the back we see King Philip IV and Queen Mariana — meaning they stand where we stand. Are we the king and queen? What is Velázquez painting? The picture turns the viewer into part of the scene. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The mirror on the back wall with the royal couple. (2) The man in the bright doorway at the back, pausing on the stairs. (3) Velázquez's chest: the red cross of the Order of Santiago, an honor he received in 1659 — so it was added after the painting was finished. ANECDOTE: The Italian painter Luca Giordano is said to have called it "the theology of painting." Picasso later painted 58 variations on it in 1957. LINK: The Rokeby Venus used a mirror to question who is looking; Las Meninas makes that question the subject of an entire masterpiece.

illustrations.title: Las Meninas
illustrations.credit: Museo del Prado, Madrid, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 어린 공주와 시녀들, 그리고 그림을 그리는 화가 자신이 등장하는 그림입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A little princess, her maids, and the painter himself at work.

notes: WHAT: "Young Woman with a Water Pitcher," oil on canvas, by Johannes Vermeer of Delft, ca. 1662. The Met, 89.15.21. A young woman in a white linen headcloth and collar opens a window with one hand and holds a silver-gilt pitcher with the other; a map hangs on the wall and a rich carpet covers the table. WHY IT MATTERS: In the Dutch Golden Age, a new middle class bought paintings of everyday life for their homes. Vermeer turned these quiet domestic moments into near-perfect studies of light. Nothing dramatic happens; the subject is the stillness itself. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The white headcloth: look for blue and gray reflections — Vermeer saw that white is never just white. (2) The pitcher and basin reflecting the colors of the carpet. (3) The light through the leaded window, falling softly across her face and the wall. ANECDOTE: Only about 35 paintings by Vermeer survive. This was the first painting by Vermeer to enter an American museum, given to The Met by Henry G. Marquand in 1889. LINK: Las Meninas showed a palace; Vermeer shows a quiet Dutch room — the drama of light without any story at all.

illustrations.title: Young Woman with a Water Pitcher
illustrations.captionKo: 창문으로 들어온 빛 속에 물병을 든 젊은 여인입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A young woman with a water pitcher, bathed in soft window light.

sectionEn: The Eighteenth Century: Rococo to Revolution
notes: WHAT: "Mezzetin," oil on canvas, by Jean-Antoine Watteau, ca. 1718–20. The Met, 34.138. Mezzetin, a stock character from Italian comedy (commedia dell'arte) — a lovesick, scheming servant — sits on a garden bench in his striped costume, playing a guitar and singing, his face turned up longingly. WHY IT MATTERS: Watteau invented the fête galante — dreamy scenes of elegant people and actors in parks — and became the first great painter of the Rococo, the light, graceful style that followed the heavy Baroque. Beneath the charm there is melancholy: pleasure is brief, and love is often unanswered. HOW TO LOOK: (1) His upturned eyes and tense hands — music as longing. (2) In the trees behind him, a marble statue of a woman with her back turned — love that will not answer. (3) The shimmering silk stripes, painted with quick, feathery strokes. ANECDOTE: Watteau was ill with tuberculosis for years and died in 1721 at just 36; his paintings' sense that happiness is fleeting has often been linked to his short life. LINK: Vermeer's quiet room gives way to Watteau's wistful garden — the 18th century begins in a soft, theatrical mood.

illustrations.title: Mezzetin
illustrations.captionKo: 이룰 수 없는 사랑을 노래하는 희극 배우 메제탱입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Mezzetin, a comedy actor, sings a song of hopeless love.

sectionEn: The Eighteenth Century: Rococo to Revolution
notes: WHAT: "The Swing" ("Les Hasards heureux de l'escarpolette" — "The Happy Accidents of the Swing"), oil on canvas, by Jean-Honoré Fragonard, 1767. Wallace Collection, London. A young woman in a frothy pink dress soars on a swing pushed by an older man in the shadows; below, a young man hidden in the bushes gazes up her skirt as her shoe flies off. WHY IT MATTERS: This is the Rococo at its most playful and flirtatious — pastel colors, lush foliage and a secret love game painted for a private patron. It is also a picture about looking: the young lover's gaze is the hidden "point" of the picture. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The flying slipper — a symbol of lost innocence. (2) The statue of Cupid on the left, finger to his lips: "Shh, it's a secret." (3) The contrast between the bright, frothy woman and the shadowy men. ANECDOTE: According to a contemporary memoir, a nobleman first asked the painter Gabriel-François Doyen to paint his mistress on a swing pushed by a bishop, with himself watching; Doyen refused and passed the commission to Fragonard. LINK: Watteau's longing turns into Fragonard's playful flirtation — and the theme of the hidden viewer, which will return with Degas, appears again.

illustrations.title: The Swing
illustrations.credit: Wallace Collection, London, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 그네를 타는 여인의 신발이 날아가고, 덤불 속 연인이 몰래 바라봅니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A woman's shoe flies off the swing as her lover secretly watches.

sectionEn: The Eighteenth Century: Rococo to Revolution
notes: WHAT: "The Death of Socrates," oil on canvas, by Jacques-Louis David, 1787. The Met, 31.45. In 399 BCE the Athenian philosopher Socrates, condemned to death for "corrupting the youth" and impiety, calmly reaches for the cup of poison hemlock while continuing to teach, his other hand pointing upward. His grieving followers surround him. WHY IT MATTERS: David led Neoclassicism, a reaction against the frivolous Rococo. He used clear outlines, sculptural bodies and a frieze-like arrangement inspired by ancient reliefs, to teach moral lessons: duty, reason and courage. Shown at the Paris Salon of 1787, just two years before the French Revolution, it praised a man who would die rather than give up his principles. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Socrates's two hands: one reaches for the cup without looking, one points up to higher truth. (2) The man handing over the cup turns away and hides his eyes. (3) Plato, seated at the foot of the bed with his back to the scene — though historically Plato was young and absent, David shows him as an old man remembering. ANECDOTE: David later became a revolutionary politician who voted for the execution of King Louis XVI, and afterward became Napoleon's official painter. LINK: Fragonard's playful swing is swept away by David's stern, heroic classicism — art returns to Greek ideals as a moral weapon.

illustrations.title: The Death of Socrates
illustrations.captionKo: 독배를 받으면서도 끝까지 가르침을 멈추지 않는 소크라테스입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Socrates calmly reaches for the poison cup while still teaching.

sectionEn: The Eighteenth Century: Rococo to Revolution
notes: WHAT: "The Nude Maja" ("La maja desnuda"), oil on canvas, by Francisco de Goya, ca. 1797–1800, and its companion "The Clothed Maja" (ca. 1800–1807; second image). Both in the Museo del Prado, Madrid. A woman reclines on a green velvet couch with her hands behind her head, looking straight at the viewer. WHY IT MATTERS: Earlier nudes hid behind myth — Venus, nymphs, biblical heroines. Goya's woman is no goddess: she is a "maja," a fashionable woman of Madrid, painted as a real person. She is often said to be among the first large Western paintings to show female pubic hair. With no mythological excuse, the nude becomes simply a real naked woman — a step toward Manet's Olympia. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Her direct, confident gaze — compare Titian's Venus of Urbino. (2) Her pose with arms behind her head, displaying rather than hiding the body. (3) Compare the two pictures: same pose, same face — the clothed version makes the naked one feel even more daring. ANECDOTE: The paintings were most likely owned by Manuel Godoy, Spain's powerful prime minister. After his fall, the Spanish Inquisition seized them, and in 1815 Goya was summoned to explain the "obscene" work. Who the model was remains unknown, despite a famous legend that she was the Duchess of Alba. LINK: David revived the ideal body; Goya strips away the ideal — a real woman, unashamed.

illustrations.title: The Nude Maja (La maja desnuda)
illustrations.credit: Museo del Prado, Madrid, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 신화의 여신이 아닌, 실제 여인을 그린 고야의 누드화입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Goya painted a real woman, not a goddess, lying on a couch.

illustrations.title: The Clothed Maja (La maja vestida)
illustrations.credit: Museo del Prado, Madrid, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 같은 자세로 옷을 입은 '옷을 입은 마하'와 비교해 보세요.
illustrations.captionEn: Compare the same woman in the same pose, but wearing clothes.

notes: WHAT: "La Grande Odalisque," oil on canvas, by Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, 1814. Musée du Louvre, Paris. Commissioned by Caroline Murat, Queen of Naples and sister of Napoleon. An odalisque (a concubine in an Ottoman harem) lies on a couch, her back to us, turning her head to look over her shoulder. WHY IT MATTERS: Ingres, David's pupil, believed in perfect line above all. But to make the line beautiful he bent anatomy: critics noticed that her back seems to have extra vertebrae, her arm is too long, and her hip impossible. It is also a key work of Orientalism — European fantasies of an exotic "East," created by artists who often had never been there (Ingres never traveled to the Middle East). HOW TO LOOK: (1) The impossibly long, smooth curve of her back. (2) Her cool, distant gaze over her shoulder. (3) The props: peacock-feather fan, turban, a hookah pipe — "exotic" signals. ANECDOTE: When shown at the Salon of 1819, critics mocked the distortions, one complaining that she had "two or three vertebrae too many." Ingres didn't care; he said that drawing is "the probity of art." LINK: Goya's maja was frankly real; Ingres's odalisque is an idealized fantasy — beauty through distortion, set in an imagined harem. Manet will answer both.

illustrations.title: La Grande Odalisque
illustrations.credit: Musée du Louvre, Paris, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 실제보다 길게 늘린 등선이 아름다운 앵그르의 '오달리스크'입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Ingres's odalisque, with a back made longer than real life.

notes: WHAT: "Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop's Grounds," oil on canvas, by John Constable, ca. 1825. The Met, 50.145.8. The tall Gothic spire of Salisbury Cathedral rises beyond an arch of dark trees, with cows drinking in a stream and a bright, cloud-filled sky. WHY IT MATTERS: Constable insisted on painting the English countryside as it really looks, from direct observation outdoors — the changing weather, wet leaves, moving clouds. He made hundreds of cloud studies ("skying") and noted the time and wind direction. This truth to nature inspired French painters (his "Hay Wain" won a gold medal at the Paris Salon of 1824) and prepared the way for Impressionism. He painted this view several times for his friend's uncle, Bishop John Fisher. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The frame of trees opening like curtains onto the cathedral. (2) The sky: clouds full of moving light. (3) Small white flecks on leaves and grass — "Constable's snow," dabs of sparkling light. ANECDOTE: The bishop reportedly disliked the dark clouds in the first version and wanted a sunnier sky, so Constable later painted a version with a calmer sky. LINK: Ingres perfected an imagined body; Constable turns to the real world outside — nature as it truly looks.

illustrations.title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop's Grounds
illustrations.captionKo: 나무 사이로 보이는 솔즈베리 대성당과 구름 낀 영국의 하늘입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Salisbury Cathedral seen through trees under a cloudy English sky.

notes: WHAT: "Liberty Leading the People (28 July 1830)," oil on canvas, by Eugène Delacroix, 1830. Musée du Louvre, Paris. During the July Revolution of 1830 in Paris, a bare-breasted woman personifying Liberty, wearing a red Phrygian cap, raises the French tricolor flag and charges over a barricade with armed citizens of every class. WHY IT MATTERS: Delacroix was the leader of French Romanticism, which valued emotion, color and movement over David's and Ingres's cool line. Here he mixes allegory (an ideal goddess-like Liberty) with gritty reality (dead bodies, smoke, ordinary Parisians). The painting became a lasting symbol of the French Republic and of revolution everywhere. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The pyramid composition with the flag at its peak. (2) The contrast between Liberty's classical, statue-like profile and the very real figures around her — a worker, a man in a top hat, a boy with pistols. (3) Notre-Dame cathedral's towers in the smoke at right. ANECDOTE: The French government bought the painting in 1831 but soon hid it from public view because it was considered too politically inflammatory. The boy with pistols is often said to have inspired the character Gavroche in Victor Hugo's Les Misérables. LINK: Constable painted calm nature; Delacroix paints passion and revolution — Romanticism at full blast.

illustrations.title: Liberty Leading the People (28 July 1830)
illustrations.credit: Musée du Louvre, Paris, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 자유의 여신이 삼색기를 들고 시민들과 함께 바리케이드를 넘습니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Liberty raises the French flag and leads people over a barricade.

notes: WHAT: "The Fighting Temeraire, tugged to her last berth to be broken up, 1838," oil on canvas, by J. M. W. Turner, 1839. National Gallery, London. A small black steam tug pulls the ghostly old warship HMS Temeraire up the Thames to be scrapped, under a blazing sunset. WHY IT MATTERS: Turner, the great English Romantic, painted light, air and atmosphere more than solid objects — a direction that leads toward Impressionism and even abstraction. The Temeraire had fought heroically at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805; here the age of sail gives way to the age of steam. It is a picture about time, loss and the industrial age. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The pale, glowing old ship vs. the dark, smoky modern tug. (2) The sunset on the right, painted with thick, fiery paint — the sun setting on an era. (3) The pale moon on the left — a quiet counterbalance. ANECDOTE: Turner called it his "darling" and refused to sell it; he left it to the nation. In 2005 it was voted Britain's greatest painting in a BBC Radio 4 poll, and since 2020 it appears with Turner's self-portrait on the Bank of England £20 note. LINK: Delacroix's color served revolution; Turner's color dissolves the world into light and mood.

illustrations.title: The Fighting Temeraire
illustrations.credit: National Gallery, London, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 낡은 군함이 증기선에 끌려 마지막 항해를 하는 노을 진 풍경입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: An old warship is towed on its last trip under a fiery sunset.

notes: WHAT: "Olympia," oil on canvas, by Édouard Manet, 1863, shown at the Paris Salon of 1865. Musée d'Orsay, Paris. A naked young woman reclines on a white bed, wearing only a black ribbon, a bracelet and a slipper, with an orchid in her hair. A Black maid brings her a bouquet (probably from a client), and a black cat arches its back at her feet. WHY IT MATTERS: Manet deliberately remade Titian's Venus of Urbino (Chapter 23) as a modern Parisian prostitute — "Olympia" was a name associated with courtesans. There is no goddess, no myth, no excuse. Her cool, businesslike stare confronts the (male) viewer as a customer. Manet also painted flatly, with harsh frontal light and few half-tones, rejecting smooth academic modeling. It caused one of the biggest scandals in art history and is often seen as a starting point of modern painting. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Her gaze — not inviting, but appraising. (2) Her hand firmly covering her lap — unlike the soft "modest Venus" gestures. (3) Titian's sleeping dog (fidelity) replaced by an alert black cat. The model was Victorine Meurent, herself a painter; the maid was modeled by a woman known as Laure. ANECDOTE: At the Salon, visitors were so outraged that guards were posted to protect the painting, and it was rehung high out of reach. In 1889–90, Claude Monet organized a public subscription to buy it for the French nation. LINK: Goya made the nude real; Manet makes it modern and confrontational — the nude now looks back and questions us.

illustrations.title: Olympia
illustrations.credit: Musée d'Orsay, Paris, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 관람자를 똑바로 바라보며 큰 스캔들을 일으킨 마네의 '올랭피아'입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Manet's Olympia stares right at us — it caused a huge scandal.

notes: WHAT: "Woman with a Parrot," oil on canvas, by Gustave Courbet, 1866. The Met, 29.100.57. A naked woman lies on a white sheet, her long dark hair spread out, playfully raising one arm to let a colorful parrot perch on her hand. WHY IT MATTERS: Courbet was the leader of Realism, famous for saying he could not paint an angel because he had never seen one. He painted laborers, funerals and real bodies. Shown at the Salon of 1866, the year after Olympia's scandal, this nude was accepted — but critics still found her too real and her pose awkward. Courbet takes the traditional reclining nude and gives it the weight and fleshiness of an actual model in a studio. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The tangled, flowing hair — sensual and unkempt, unlike Ingres's smooth perfection. (2) The real heaviness of the body sinking into the sheets. (3) The bright parrot against dark trees: a flash of color and a hint of playful desire. ANECDOTE: The painting was later bought by the American collectors Henry and Louisine Havemeyer and came to The Met with their great bequest in 1929 — the same collection that brought The Met many of its Degas works. LINK: Manet challenged the nude with a stare; Courbet challenges it with sheer physical reality.

illustrations.title: Woman with a Parrot
illustrations.captionKo: 앵무새와 놀고 있는 여인을 사실적으로 그린 쿠르베의 누드화입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Courbet's realistic nude woman playing with a parrot.

notes: WHAT: "The Cradle," oil on canvas, by Berthe Morisot, 1872. Musée d'Orsay, Paris. Morisot's sister Edma watches over her sleeping baby daughter Blanche, who lies in a cradle draped with a sheer white veil. WHY IT MATTERS: Morisot was a founding member of the Impressionists and the only woman to exhibit in their first group show in 1874, where this painting was shown. Women artists of the time could not easily paint in cafés or public streets, so Morisot made the private world of women — home, children, gardens — into serious modern art. Her quick, feathery brushwork is among the freest of the group. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The diagonal of the mother's arm and the curtain's diagonal, which meet at the baby. (2) The transparent veil — painted with a few light strokes. (3) Edma's gaze: tender, but also thoughtful; Edma had given up painting when she married. ANECDOTE: Morisot married Eugène Manet, Édouard Manet's brother, in 1874. She had also modeled for Édouard in several famous paintings. LINK: After Courbet's and Manet's provocations, a group of young painters began working outside the official Salon — Impressionism begins, and a woman stands among its founders.

illustrations.title: The Cradle
illustrations.credit: Musée d'Orsay, Paris, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 잠든 아기를 바라보는 엄마의 다정한 모습입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A mother gently watches her baby sleeping in a cradle.

notes: WHAT: "Impression, Sunrise," oil on canvas, by Claude Monet, 1872. Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris. The harbor of Le Havre at dawn: blue-gray mist, dim cranes and ships, small dark boats, and a bright orange sun with its reflection on the water. WHY IT MATTERS: This painting gave Impressionism its name. When it was shown in the first independent group exhibition in Paris in 1874, the critic Louis Leroy mocked the artists as "Impressionists" in the satirical paper Le Charivari, saying wallpaper in its first state was more finished. The artists adopted the name. Impressionists painted quickly, often outdoors, to capture fleeting effects of light and atmosphere rather than detailed objects. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The quick, visible brushstrokes — nothing is "finished" in the academic sense. (2) The orange sun and its broken reflection: a few strokes that glow. (3) Compare the second image, Monet's "Stacks of Wheat (End of Summer)" (1890–91, Art Institute of Chicago): later he painted the same subject again and again to show how light changes everything. ANECDOTE: The painting was stolen from the Musée Marmottan in 1985 and recovered in 1990. LINK: Morisot painted intimacy; Monet painted an instant of light — and named a movement.

illustrations.title: Impression, Sunrise
illustrations.credit: Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: '인상주의'라는 이름이 생겨난, 새벽 항구의 붉은 해입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: An orange sunrise over a harbor — the painting that named Impressionism.

illustrations.title: Stacks of Wheat (End of Summer)
illustrations.captionKo: 모네는 같은 짚더미를 여러 번 그려 빛의 변화를 보여 주었습니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Monet painted the same wheat stacks many times to show changing light.

notes: WHAT: "The Dance Class," oil on canvas, by Edgar Degas, 1874. The Met, 1987.47.1. In a pale green rehearsal room of the Paris Opéra ballet, young dancers in white tutus wait, stretch, fix their hair and practice, while the elderly ballet master Jules Perrot — once a famous dancer himself — leans on his tall stick. Mothers sit on a staircase at the back. WHY IT MATTERS: Degas (1834–1917), son of a Parisian banking family, exhibited with the Impressionists but preferred to call himself a Realist or "Independent." He rarely painted outdoors; he composed carefully in his studio from many drawings. Dancers became his great subject: not the glamour of the performance, but the waiting, the work and the tired bodies behind it. Many dancers were working-class girls called "petits rats" (little rats). HOW TO LOOK: (1) The off-center, "snapshot" composition: the floor opens up a big empty space and figures are cut by the frame — ideas Degas took from Japanese prints and photography. (2) In front, a dancer with a red flower in her hair looks down, lost in her own thoughts, half-hidden by a music stand. (3) The double bass cropped at the lower left edge, and the mirror reflecting a window and other dancers. ANECDOTE: Although the scene looks like a spontaneous glimpse, Degas assembled it in his studio from many separate drawings of dancers who posed for him, arranging them like a stage director. LINK: Monet chased outdoor light; Degas turns to modern indoor life and the working bodies of dancers — the first of our three Degas chapters.

illustrations.title: The Dance Class
illustrations.captionKo: 발레 선생님과 연습을 기다리는 어린 무용수들의 모습입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Young ballet dancers wait and practice while their teacher watches.

notes: WHAT: "Dance at the Moulin de la Galette," oil on canvas, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, 1876. Musée d'Orsay, Paris. On a Sunday afternoon at an open-air dance hall in Montmartre, crowds of young Parisians dance, talk and drink under trees, dappled with sunlight. WHY IT MATTERS: Renoir painted the pleasure of modern leisure — ordinary working and artistic Parisians enjoying themselves. He shows how sunlight filtered through leaves breaks into spots of color on clothes, faces and the ground. His friends posed for many of the figures, and he is said to have worked on the large canvas on site, carrying it there with friends' help. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The spots of light and shadow on the dark jackets and pink and blue dresses. (2) The soft, blurry faces in the background — the crowd dissolves into movement. (3) The striped dress of the girl in the foreground, leaning toward a friend. ANECDOTE: The painting belonged to the painter and collector Gustave Caillebotte, who bequeathed it to the French state. A smaller version sold in 1990 for about $78 million, then one of the highest prices ever paid for a painting. LINK: Degas showed the hard work behind the dance; Renoir shows the joy of dancing in the sun.

illustrations.title: Dance at the Moulin de la Galette
illustrations.credit: Musée d'Orsay, Paris, via Wikimedia Commons
illustrations.captionKo: 햇빛이 나뭇잎 사이로 반짝이는 몽마르트르의 일요일 무도회입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: A sunny Sunday dance party in Montmartre, with light through the trees.

notes: WHAT: "Paris Street; Rainy Day," oil on canvas, by Gustave Caillebotte, 1877. Art Institute of Chicago, 1964.336. Well-dressed Parisians with umbrellas cross a wet cobblestone intersection (the Place de Dublin, near the Saint-Lazare train station), with new, uniform apartment buildings behind them. WHY IT MATTERS: In the 1850s–60s, Baron Haussmann rebuilt Paris with wide boulevards and uniform buildings. Caillebotte painted this brand-new modern city, where strangers pass each other without contact. Unlike the loose brushwork of Monet, his surface is smooth and precise, almost photographic — showing how varied Impressionism was. It was shown at the third Impressionist exhibition in 1877. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The green lamppost that splits the painting in two. (2) The couple at right walking toward us — and the man about to bump umbrellas with them. (3) The shining wet cobblestones and the deep perspective of the streets. ANECDOTE: Caillebotte was wealthy; he financially supported his friends Monet, Renoir and others, and bought their paintings. His bequest of these works to France (1894) helped bring Impressionism into the national museums. LINK: Renoir's sunny dance hall gives way to Caillebotte's cool, rainy modern street — two faces of the new Paris.

illustrations.title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
illustrations.captionKo: 비 오는 날, 우산을 쓴 사람들이 새로 지은 파리 거리를 걷습니다.
illustrations.captionEn: People with umbrellas walk through a new Paris street on a rainy day.

notes: WHAT: "The Little Fourteen-Year-Old Dancer" (also called "Little Dancer, Aged Fourteen"), by Edgar Degas. The original, in wax with real hair, fabric and a satin ribbon, was made around 1878–81; this bronze was cast in 1922, after Degas's death, and dressed with a cotton tutu and silk hair ribbon. The Met, 29.100.370. WHY IT MATTERS: This was the only sculpture Degas ever exhibited, at the sixth Impressionist exhibition in 1881, shown in a glass case like a scientific specimen. It shocked viewers: real clothes and hair on a sculpture, and a working-class ballet student shown with her chin up, eyes half-closed, not idealized at all. Some critics called her ugly. The model was Marie van Goethem, a young student of the Paris Opéra ballet school. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The pose: hands clasped behind her back, one foot forward in fourth position — tired but proud. (2) The real fabric tutu and ribbon against the metal body. (3) Her face, tilted up — confident, or defiant? NORTON SIMON CONNECTION: The Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena owns more than 100 works by Degas, one of the largest public Degas collections in the world. Norton Simon acquired the set of bronze "modèles" (the master casts from which Degas's other bronzes were made), and the museum displays a cast of this Little Dancer. Degas's sculptures were wax and clay studies found in his studio after his death in 1917; his heirs had more than 70 of them cast in bronze. ANECDOTE: The original wax figure is now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington. LINK: From painting dancers to modeling one in three dimensions — the second Degas chapter, and the one that leads straight to Pasadena.

illustrations.title: The Little Fourteen-Year-Old Dancer
illustrations.captionKo: 진짜 천 치마와 리본을 단 드가의 조각, '14세의 어린 무용수'입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Degas's "Little Dancer," a sculpture wearing a real cloth tutu and ribbon.

notes: WHAT: "The Thinker," bronze, by Auguste Rodin, modeled ca. 1880, this cast ca. 1910 (about 70 cm high). The Met, 11.173.9. A muscular naked man sits on a rock, chin on his hand, deep in thought. WHY IT MATTERS: Rodin was the greatest sculptor of the 19th century and brought new life to the nude body in sculpture. The Thinker began as part of "The Gates of Hell," a giant bronze doorway commissioned in 1880 and based on Dante's Divine Comedy. The figure originally represented Dante himself, seated above the gates, imagining his poem; it was first called "The Poet." Rodin used the strong male nude of Michelangelo (Chapter 21) to express not action but intense thought. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The whole body is thinking: clenched toes, tense back, right elbow on the left knee — a twisted, uncomfortable pose. (2) The rough, modeled surface that catches light — Rodin's fingerprints in clay translated into bronze. (3) Walk around it (or imagine doing so): it changes from every angle. NORTON SIMON CONNECTION: A large cast of The Thinker stands at the front of the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, greeting visitors near the entrance among other Rodin sculptures. ANECDOTE: Rodin's early statue "The Age of Bronze" (1877) was so lifelike that critics accused him of casting it directly from a living model. LINK: Degas's Little Dancer brought modern reality into sculpture; Rodin brought emotion and inner life into the nude body.

illustrations.title: The Thinker
illustrations.captionKo: 바위에 앉아 깊은 생각에 잠긴 로댕의 '생각하는 사람'입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Rodin's "Thinker" sits on a rock, lost in deep thought.

notes: WHAT: "A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884," oil on canvas, by Georges Seurat, painted 1884–86, with a painted border added 1888–89. Art Institute of Chicago, 1926.224. Parisians of different classes relax on a sunny island in the Seine river — couples, soldiers, children, a woman fishing, a lady walking a monkey on a leash. WHY IT MATTERS: Seurat wanted to make Impressionism scientific and lasting. He used pointillism (or divisionism): tiny dots of pure color placed side by side, so they mix in the viewer's eye. His figures are stiff and still, like ancient Egyptian or Greek reliefs — calm, frozen and timeless instead of fleeting. It was shown at the eighth and last Impressionist exhibition in 1886, where it caused a sensation. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Step close to see the dots, then step back to see them blend. (2) The profiles — almost every figure is shown in strict side view or front view. (3) The odd details: the monkey, the woman fishing, the trumpet player — there are many small mysteries. ANECDOTE: Seurat spent about two years on it, making dozens of drawings and oil sketches. He died in 1891 at just 31. LINK: Rodin's rough, living surfaces vs. Seurat's ordered dots — artists after Impressionism look for new structure.

illustrations.title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884
illustrations.captionKo: 작은 점들로 그린, 센강 섬에서 쉬는 파리 사람들의 일요일 오후입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Parisians relax on an island on a Sunday, painted with tiny dots.

notes: WHAT: "Woman Bathing in a Shallow Tub," charcoal and pastel on paper, by Edgar Degas, 1885. The Met, 29.100.41 (H. O. Havemeyer Collection). A naked woman bends over in a shallow round washtub, seen from slightly above, washing herself, absorbed in her task. WHY IT MATTERS: In the 1880s Degas made a long series of women bathing, drying and combing their hair, mostly in pastel. At the eighth Impressionist exhibition in 1886 he showed a group of these nudes. They broke with the whole tradition of the nude we have followed: no goddess, no myth, no harem, no pose for the viewer — and, unlike Olympia, no gaze back at us. These women seem unaware of being seen. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The high viewpoint, looking down into the tub — we are close, and a little intrusive. (2) The awkward, natural bend of the back and arms: a body doing something, not displaying itself. (3) The pastel strokes: Degas layered and crosshatched chalky color, leaving the marks visible. ANECDOTE: According to the writer George Moore, Degas said that the nude had always been shown in poses that assume an audience, but his women were simple people busy with their bodies — "It is as if you looked through a keyhole." That "keyhole" idea is both the beauty and the problem of these works. LINK: Our third Degas chapter: the nude thread reaches its most intimate point — from Venus who knows she is seen to a woman who doesn't.

illustrations.title: Woman Bathing in a Shallow Tub
illustrations.captionKo: 목욕통에서 몸을 씻는 여인을 위에서 내려다본 드가의 파스텔화입니다.
illustrations.captionEn: Degas looks down on a woman washing in a tub, unaware of us.

notes: WHAT: "The Starry Night," oil on canvas, by Vincent van Gogh, June 1889. Museum of Modern Art, New York. A swirling night sky with eleven glowing stars and a crescent moon spreads over a quiet village; a dark, flame-like cypress tree rises in the foreground. WHY IT MATTERS: Van Gogh (1853–1890) used color and thick, rhythmic brushstrokes to express feeling, not just to record what he saw — a key step toward Expressionism. He painted it while staying voluntarily at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, after a mental health crisis. The view is based on what he saw from his window before sunrise, but the village and the church steeple were added from imagination and memory. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The great spiral in the center of the sky — energy you can almost feel moving. (2) The cypress tree, linking earth and sky; cypresses were associated with death and eternity. (3) The calm, small village below, with lit windows, against the cosmic movement above. ANECDOTE: In his letters to his brother Theo, Vincent wrote about the morning star (Venus) he saw from his window — astronomers confirm Venus was bright in that eastern sky in spring 1889. He died the following year, at 37. LINK: Seurat ordered color scientifically; Van Gogh set it free to express emotion.

notes: WHAT: "The Child's Bath," oil on canvas, by Mary Cassatt, 1893. Art Institute of Chicago, 1910.2. A mother in a striped dress holds a little girl on her lap and gently washes her feet in a basin; both look down at the water. WHY IT MATTERS: Cassatt (1844–1926), born in Pennsylvania, was the only American to exhibit with the Impressionists in Paris — invited by Degas, who became her friend and mentor. She made the bond between mothers and children her great subject, painting it with seriousness, not sentimentality. After seeing a large exhibition of Japanese prints in Paris in 1890, she adopted their high viewpoints, flat patterns and strong outlines, which you can see here. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The high viewpoint, looking down on the pair — just like Degas's bathers, but now about care, not secrecy. (2) The bold stripes of the dress against the child's soft skin. (3) The two heads bending together — the mother's and child's gazes meet at the same point: the feet in the water. ANECDOTE: Cassatt advised her friends Louisine and Henry Havemeyer on buying art; that is how many of The Met's Degas works (including the bather in Chapter 53) came to New York. LINK: Degas showed a woman bathing alone, seen as if through a keyhole; Cassatt, his friend, shows bathing as tenderness — a woman artist's answer.

notes: WHAT: "The Basket of Apples," oil on canvas, by Paul Cézanne, about 1893. Art Institute of Chicago, 1926.252. A tilted basket of apples, a wine bottle, a plate of biscuits and a crumpled white cloth on a table. WHY IT MATTERS: Cézanne (1839–1906) wanted to make "something solid and durable" from Impressionism. He studied simple objects for weeks and painted them as if seen from several viewpoints at once. The table edges don't line up, the bottle leans, the plate tips toward us — but the picture feels balanced. This breaking of single-point perspective (the system used since the Renaissance, Chapter 22) opened the way for Cubism and modern art. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The front edge of the table: it is at a different height on the left and right of the cloth. (2) The tilted bottle and the plate seen from above. (3) The apples, built from patches of color, feel heavy and round. ANECDOTE: Cézanne reportedly said, "I want to astonish Paris with an apple." Picasso and Matisse later called him something like "the father of us all." LINK: Cassatt borrowed Japanese flatness; Cézanne rebuilt space itself — the old rules of perspective begin to break.

notes: WHAT: "Two Tahitian Women," oil on canvas, by Paul Gauguin, 1899. The Met, 49.58.1. Two young Tahitian women stand close together against a flat green and yellow background; one, bare-breasted, holds a tray of red flowers (often identified as mango blossoms). WHY IT MATTERS: Gauguin (1848–1903) left Paris for Tahiti in 1891, searching for a "primitive" paradise away from modern Europe. He used flat areas of bold, non-natural color and simplified forms, deeply influencing modern art. His nudes and half-nudes of Tahitian women continue the reclining-and-offering nude tradition, now placed in an imagined tropical Eden. Today they are also discussed critically: Gauguin projected European fantasies onto Polynesian women, and he had relationships with very young Tahitian girls — a clear example of what John Berger later called the question of "who is looking" (see the Epilogue). HOW TO LOOK: (1) The flat background — no deep space, like a decorative panel. (2) The offering gesture with the flowers, echoing paintings of Eve or Venus. (3) Their calm, inward faces: do they look at us, or past us? ANECDOTE: Gauguin had worked as a stockbroker before becoming a full-time painter. He spent two difficult months with Van Gogh in Arles in 1888, ending when Van Gogh cut off part of his own ear. LINK: Cézanne remade space; Gauguin remade color — and carried the nude into a European dream of the South Seas.

notes: WHAT: "The Kiss" ("Der Kuss"), oil and gold leaf on canvas, by Gustav Klimt, 1907–08. Österreichische Galerie Belvedere, Vienna. A couple embraces on the edge of a flowery meadow, wrapped together in a single golden cloak; the man bends to kiss the woman's cheek as she kneels with closed eyes. WHY IT MATTERS: Klimt (1862–1918) was a founder of the Vienna Secession (1897), a group of artists who broke away from the conservative academy. In his "Golden Period" he used real gold leaf and flat ornamental patterns, inspired partly by the Byzantine mosaics he saw in Ravenna in 1903 — a link back to the gold of medieval art (Chapters 12–13). The bodies are almost hidden, yet the painting is full of sensual feeling. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The patterns: hard black-and-white rectangles on the man's robe, soft circles and flowers on the woman's dress. (2) Only faces, hands and feet are painted "realistically"; everything else is flat ornament. (3) The edge of the cliff and flowers under her feet — a hint of danger in the bliss. ANECDOTE: The Austrian state bought the painting in 1908, while it was being shown at the Kunstschau exhibition in Vienna — even before Klimt had officially finished it, according to some accounts. LINK: Gauguin dreamed of paradise in the tropics; Klimt finds it in a golden embrace in Vienna.

notes: WHAT: "Nude," charcoal on paper, by Egon Schiele, 1917. The Met, 1984.433.286. A naked woman sits with one knee raised, her arm across her chest and her hand lifted to her hair, drawn with a few sure, wiry lines on bare paper. WHY IT MATTERS: Schiele (1890–1918) was Klimt's younger protégé in Vienna, but where Klimt wrapped bodies in gold, Schiele stripped them bare. His lines are nervous, angular and unflattering; his nudes (including many of himself) are thin, twisted, frank and often uncomfortable. He drew the body as a site of desire, anxiety and mortality — Expressionism in its rawest form. His drawings are among the most direct images of the body in all of Western art. HOW TO LOOK: (1) The continuous outline — almost no shading; one line does everything. (2) The empty paper around her: no room, no story, just a person. (3) The gesture of the arm across the chest — a modern echo of the ancient "modest Venus," now self-conscious rather than graceful. ANECDOTE: In 1912 Schiele was jailed for about three weeks; he was convicted of displaying erotic drawings where children could see them. In October 1918 he died of the Spanish flu at 28, just three days after his pregnant wife, Edith — and the same year as his mentor Klimt. LINK: Klimt covered the body in gold; Schiele leaves it naked and vulnerable — the end of our journey through the 19th century and the First World War.

illustrations.captionEn: Schiele drew this nude with just a few sharp, nervous lines.

notes: WHAT: "Breakfast after the Bath," pastel on paper laid down on board, by Edgar Degas, 1895/98. Art Institute of Chicago, 1999.365. A woman, seen from behind, bends forward as she steps out of her bath, drying herself; a clothed maid stands at left, bringing her a morning drink (as the title says). The second image is a late charcoal by Degas, "After the Bath" (c. 1900, Art Institute of Chicago), where only line and gesture remain. WHY IT MATTERS (AND HOW TO LOOK AT A NUDE): In The Nude (1956), the art historian Kenneth Clark distinguished being naked — "deprived of our clothes," exposed and embarrassed — from the nude, a body transformed by art into an ideal, confident form. Our journey followed that ideal from the kouros and Aphrodite through Botticelli, Titian and Ingres. In Ways of Seeing (1972), John Berger answered: "To be naked is to be oneself. To be nude is to be seen naked by others and yet not recognized for oneself." He pointed out that most European nudes were made by men for male owners: "men act and women appear." Olympia's stare, the Rokeby Venus's mirror, and Degas's "keyhole" all make us ask who is looking, and why. HOW TO LOOK: (1) Her back is turned; she ignores us completely — is that respect for her privacy, or the voyeur's advantage? (2) The late Degas colors: bold oranges, greens and pinks, thick strokes, done as his eyesight was failing. (3) The maid: the scene is domestic and ordinary, not mythological. ANECDOTE: Degas returned to the bather-and-maid theme in several versions in the 1890s. The bathers and dancers in the Norton Simon Museum's large Degas collection in Pasadena come from this same lifelong search — standing before them, you stand right where the debate between Clark and Berger lives. LINK: After Schiele's raw nudes, we return to Degas, where the story of the modern nude truly begins — and where this reader's own story with art began.
